meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There isn't anyone you couldn't love once you've heard their story'?
meta.ogDescription: Not originally Mr. Rogers — the words are Benedictine sister Mary Lou Kownacki's, documented in 1994. Rogers carried and popularized them.

answer.label: Not Fred Rogers — actually Mary Lou Kownacki
answer.sourceLine: The line is a fragment of a prayer by Benedictine sister Mary Lou Kownacki — “Engrave this upon my heart: There isn’t anyone you couldn’t love once you’ve heard their story.” Fred Rogers carried a copy of it and loved to share it, which is how it drifted onto his name, but per Quote Investigator the words are Kownacki’s, first documented in 1994.

source.excerpt: Engrave this upon my heart: There isn’t anyone you couldn’t love once you’ve heard their story.
trail: The definitive trace is Quote Investigator’s 2022 entry, which finds the earliest strong match in the 1994 anthology More Random Acts of Kindness, attributing it to Mary Lou Kownacki, OSB.
In The World According to Mister Rogers (2003), the saying appears with a note that Fred Rogers “loved especially — and carried around with him” this quote by Kownacki, per his wife Joanne’s framing.
Mary Lou Kownacki (1941–2023) was a Benedictine sister of Erie, poet, and peace activist — long a writing partner and “muse” to Sister Joan Chittister.
source.excerptNote: The famous line is the second half of Kownacki’s prayer; a separate 2003 compilation, Worth Repeating, swapped “my” for “thy” in the opening clause.

author.name: Mary Lou Kownacki, OSB
author.heading: Who was Mary Lou Kownacki?
author.bio: Mary Lou Kownacki was a Benedictine sister of Erie, Pennsylvania, a poet and lifelong peace activist who led Pax Christi USA and Benedictines for Peace. She was also a close collaborator and “muse” to Sister Joan Chittister. Her prayer-line about hearing another’s story became famous after Fred Rogers adopted and shared it.

misattribution.heading: How it became a “Mister Rogers” quote
misattribution.intro: Fred Rogers admired this line so much that he carried it with him and quoted it — and because his name is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for feel-good sayings, the words were gradually reassigned to him.

items.why: Countless quote sites and social posts print the line under Rogers’ name. He genuinely loved and shared it, but Quote Investigator shows the wording predates his use and belongs to Kownacki.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Mary Lou Kownacki’s, first documented in 1994; Rogers carried and popularized them, and his wife Joanne credited Kownacki in the 2003 foreword to The World According to Mister Rogers, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it resonated
lead: The sentence works as a compact plea for empathy: it argues that understanding someone’s history dissolves the distance that makes them easy to dislike. Kownacki wrote it as a prayer — a thing to engrave on the heart — which is why it reads as a moral discipline rather than a slogan.

Fred Rogers, whose whole vocation was helping children see the humanity in others, found it irresistible and carried it with him. His endorsement gave the line a second life and, ironically, a second author.
